claims.text: The initial high-entropy alloy is a single-phase solid solution.
Adding an unspecified element or applying an unspecified processing route will improve toughness after thermal exposure and subsequent loading.
The intervention changes grain size and grain-size distribution.
The intervention causes precipitate or secondary-phase formation.
The intervention produces a stable single-phase solid solution.
Reduced grain size and altered grain-size distribution contribute to improved toughness.
Formation of precipitates contributes to improved toughness.
Reduction of defects contributes to improved toughness.
A stable single-phase solid solution contributes to improved toughness after thermal exposure and loading.
The intervened alloy will have greater toughness than the same alloy tested under identical conditions without the intervention.
The hypothesis applies under thermal exposure followed by loading.
Applicability depends on the composition, processing route, and thermal-exposure conditions.
Failure to observe greater toughness in the intervened alloy than in the untreated control would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The alloy is already described as a single-phase solid solution, while the mechanism says the intervention achieves formation of that state, leaving unclear what phase-state change the intervention causes.

The proposed mechanism simultaneously invokes a stable single-phase solid solution and precipitate formation; ordinary precipitates constitute an additional phase unless a coherent single-phase-compatible interpretation is specified.
